questions.question: A customer can place many orders, but each order belongs to one customer. Where should the foreign key live?
options: On orders as customer_id
On customers as order_id
In a comma-separated order_ids column
In a junction table with no foreign keys
questions.explanation: The foreign key belongs on the many side. Each order row can name exactly one owning customer, and the database can enforce that parent relationship.

questions.question: Why does a project membership usually need a junction table?
options: It is the standard solution for a many-to-many relationship and can store membership facts such as role
It makes foreign keys unnecessary
It turns every user into a project owner
It avoids all indexes
questions.explanation: A junction row connects one user to one project. It represents the relationship itself and can carry attributes that do not belong to either endpoint.

questions.question: Why store unit_price_cents on an order item when products already have a current price?
options: To preserve the price actually charged when the product price later changes
To remove the need for a product table
Because every price must be duplicated everywhere
To make foreign keys optional
questions.explanation: The order-item price is a transaction fact. It preserves historical correctness without pretending that it is the product's current catalog price.

questions.question: For a query that filters by customer_id and returns the newest orders first, which index best matches the access path?
options: (customer_id, created_at DESC)
(created_at, customer_id)
(status)
No index because the result page is small
questions.explanation: Leading with customer_id narrows to one customer's rows, and the created_at direction supports returning the newest rows without an additional sort.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a read projection?
options: A derived, rebuildable copy optimized for a specific read
The only place a payment write should be stored
A replacement for all database constraints
An unowned cache that never needs monitoring
questions.explanation: A projection trades duplicate storage and freshness work for a cheaper read. It needs an owner, update path, monitoring, and a rebuild plan.

questions.question: What is the safer sequence for making a newly required column on a large production table?
options: Add it nullable, deploy compatible code, backfill and validate it, then enforce NOT NULL
Make it required first and repair production errors afterward
Delete the old column before any application deployment
Skip validation because the migration succeeded locally
questions.explanation: Staged migrations keep old and new application versions compatible while data is backfilled and validated.
